id: Your Invitation to a Modest Breakfast

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

It’s too cold to smoke outside, but if you come over, I’ll keep my hands to myself, or won’t I. I would like to tell you about the wall eaten up by the climbing plant—it was so beautiful. Various things have been happening to me, all of them sexual. The man on the bus took off his pants so I could see him better. Another man said, “Ignore him darlin’. Just sit on my lap.” But I’m not one of those who’s hungriest in the morning, unlike the man at the bakery who eats egg after egg after egg. Listen. Come over: the cold has already eaten the summer. I need another pair of ears: from the kitchen I can’t tell if I’m hearing wind chimes or some gray woman with failing arms dropping a pan full of onions and potatoes. This morning I need four hands— two to wash the greens, one to lift a teakettle, one to pour the milk. This morning, one little mouth will not do. We could play a game where we crouch on the tiles, two yellow dogs drinking coffee from bowls. We could play a game where we let the breakfast burn. Outside there’s a world where every love scene begins with a man in a doorway; he walks over to the woman and says “Open your mouth.”

outputs.L2:
The weather is too bitter for smoking outdoors. Still, if you visit, perhaps I’ll behave and keep my hands off you—though perhaps not. I want to describe the vine-devoured wall; it was astonishingly lovely. Lately, one thing after another has happened to me, and every incident has been sexual. On the bus, a man removed his trousers to give me a clearer view of him. A second man told me, “Don’t pay attention to him, sweetheart. Come sit on my lap instead.”

Unlike the bakery customer who devours egg after egg after egg, I’m not among those whose appetite is strongest at daybreak. Listen to me. Come here—the cold has consumed what remained of summer. I need an extra set of ears, because from the kitchen I can’t distinguish between the sound of wind chimes and that of some gray-haired woman, her arms weakening, letting a pan of onions and potatoes fall.

Today I require four hands: a pair for rinsing the greens, another to raise the teakettle, and a final one to pour the milk. A single small mouth is insufficient this morning. We might invent a game in which we squat on the tiled floor like two yellow dogs, lapping coffee from bowls. Or we could pretend that allowing breakfast to scorch is part of the game.

Beyond these walls is a world where each romantic scene starts with a man standing in a doorway. He approaches the woman and tells her, “Open your mouth.”
outputs.L3:
The speaker begins by inviting another person to come in from the cold, using a teasing suggestion of physical intimacy to make the offer feel both playful and urgent. Throughout the passage, memories of natural beauty are set against a series of unsettling, sexualized encounters with men. This contrast complicates the speaker’s recollections: the surrounding world may be beautiful, but it is also shaped by intrusive male desire and sexual demands.

Images of cold and hunger reinforce the sense that summer has ended. They suggest not only physical discomfort but also emotional deprivation, emphasizing the speaker’s longing for warmth, safety, and companionship. In response to this loneliness, the speaker imagines sharing the morning with another person. She needs the other person’s ears, hands, and mouth—both to experience the morning’s sensations and to participate in its ordinary tasks.

As a result, domestic scenes such as preparing and eating breakfast become playful and intimate. Simple acts are transformed into opportunities for closeness, cooperation, and sensual connection. These private moments offer a striking contrast to the wider world of male sexual pressure: rather than being demanding or threatening, the imagined intimacy is mutual, comforting, and rooted in everyday care.
outputs.L4:
The speaker constructs a world in which coldness, domesticity, sexuality, and longing continually overlap. Familiar objects and household spaces do not provide uncomplicated comfort; instead, they become part of a surreal sensory landscape marked by bodily need and emotional exposure. Images of food, warmth, skin, and shelter suggest that intimacy is as necessary as nourishment. At the same time, the cold surrounding these scenes conveys isolation, making the desire for another person feel urgent and almost physical.

Sexual encounters in this world are not presented as purely romantic or liberating. They are shaped by hunger, vulnerability, and the pressure of male presence. Men enter or occupy intimate spaces in ways that complicate the speaker’s relationship to her own body and desires. Their intrusion creates an atmosphere in which closeness can bring danger as well as comfort, and in which the boundaries between affection, appetite, and power remain unstable. The surreal quality of the imagery intensifies this uncertainty: ordinary domestic details become strange, while bodily experience is transformed into something dreamlike and unsettling.

Against this background, the speaker’s invitation to intimacy carries particular emotional weight. She is not simply expressing sexual desire; she is asking for companionship, recognition, and shared warmth in a world that often feels inhospitable. Her longing emerges from a need to resist loneliness and to create a private space where vulnerability might be met with tenderness rather than exploitation. Yet the invitation remains uneasy because intimacy has already been shaped by intrusion and unequal power. The person she addresses therefore represents both a desired companion and the possibility of a different kind of closeness—one based on mutual presence rather than possession.

By intertwining cold domestic imagery with sensual and surreal scenes, the text portrays desire as both sustaining and precarious. Intimacy offers the promise of warmth, but it cannot be separated from the speaker’s awareness of hunger, exposure, and male interference. Her longing is therefore deeply ambivalent: it expresses hope for connection while acknowledging the risks that closeness can carry. Ultimately, the speaker’s desire for another person becomes a search for refuge—a way of imagining tenderness within a world where the body is always vulnerable and where companionship may be the only protection against emotional and physical cold.

**Various Perspectives**

The world can be understood in various ways. One person may see a challenge as an obstacle, while another views it as an opportunity to grow. The difference often comes from experience, values, and imagination. By listening to one another, we discover new perspectives and make better decisions.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, sensual prose poem in the voice of a lonely speaker inviting someone over on a freezing morning, blending breakfast imagery, dark humor, sexual encounters, and an unsettling final scene.
counterfactuals.output:
Come over. The morning has frozen its tongue to the windows, and the radiator is rehearsing its tiny metallic death. I have made coffee black enough to contain weather. There are eggs in the pan, two pale suns with their eyes still open, and toast burned into little memorial plaques.

Come hungry.

I have set a place for you beside the knife. The grapefruit waits like a blushing planet, halved and sugared. Outside, the cars wear white shrouds; the pigeons look unemployed. Even the church across the street has pulled its steeple deeper into its coat.

We could eat with our fingers. We could laugh about the landlord, about mortality, about how the smoke alarm only sings when I try to care for someone. You could warm your hands beneath my shirt. I could find the cold places on you and persuade them, slowly, to confess.

Last time, in the hotel, we left our clothes in a trail so orderly it looked like evidence. In the shower, your mouth tasted of pennies and rain. Later, the ceiling fan turned above us like a bored executioner, and we invented new names for loneliness, each one less accurate than the last.

Come over before the syrup hardens.

The bed is unmade in the shape of an accident. The sheets remember every body badly. I have lit a candle that smells like vanilla and arson. If you arrive, I promise not to ask where you have been, or whose fingerprints bloom beneath your ribs. I will only open the door and let the winter stare.

We will eat. We will undress. We will make our brief animal argument against the cold.

And afterward, when the light turns blue and the coffee forms a skin, I will show you what has been knocking all morning from inside the freezer.

Do not be afraid.

It is only my heart, wrapped in butcher paper, still beating whenever someone climbs the stairs.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical monologue that begins with “It’s too cold to smoke outside” and explores desire, loneliness, urban encounters, domestic chores, and the wish for another body in the kitchen.
counterfactuals.output:
It’s too cold to smoke outside, so I stand at the window with the match unstruck, holding the cigarette like a small white promise I no longer believe. Below, the city keeps introducing strangers to one another beneath umbrellas—shoulders brushing, apologies rising in little clouds, taxis carrying warm silhouettes from one lit room to the next.

All evening I have been wanting without an object. Or perhaps the object keeps changing: the woman on the train who slept against the glass, the man at the corner store who called me darling without looking up, the upstairs neighbor laughing through the pipes. Desire is a light moving behind curtains. You see it, then lose it, then imagine the whole room.

I come home and do what must be done. I rinse the plates. I fold the towels into obedient squares. I sweep onion skin and salt from the floor. The refrigerator hums with the patience of an animal that knows I will eventually open it and stare inside. There are carrots going soft, half a lemon, a jar of mustard, all the ingredients of a life maintained rather than lived.

Loneliness is not silence. It is the radiator knocking. It is the spoon dropped in the sink and no one asking what happened. It is catching your reflection in the dark window and mistaking it, for one bright second, for someone who has come to visit.

What I want is simple enough to embarrass me: another body in the kitchen. Someone barefoot on the cold tile, tasting the sauce from the wooden spoon. Someone reaching past me for a glass, making the narrow room narrower. I want to say careful, it’s hot. I want our hips to touch by accident and then, because we are tired of accidents, on purpose.

Outside, the city goes on exchanging its lonely people. Inside, I light the stove. Blue flame, blue hour. I chop garlic finely, as if devotion were a thing that could be prepared.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental prose poem about cold weather, climbing plants, public sexual harassment, a hungry bakery customer, wind chimes, onions and potatoes, and two people pretending to be yellow dogs drinking coffee.
counterfactuals.output:
Cold arrives without knocking, slips its white hand under every door. The climbing plants, confused by the sky’s hard face, keep reaching—green cursive on brick, a sentence refusing its period.

At the bus stop, a man whistles at a woman as if she were weather he had ordered. His words follow her down the pavement, cheap hooks. She does not turn. Above them, wind chimes strike their small aluminum alarms: not music, exactly, but witnesses.

Inside the bakery, someone hungry presses both palms to the glass. Croissants shine like folded suns. *Please,* the customer says, though no one has asked a question. In the back room, onions and potatoes wait in burlap darkness, practicing their underground patience.

At the corner table, we pretend to be yellow dogs drinking coffee. We lap carefully from porcelain cups, tails imagined, ears bright with frost. You say *good dog* to me; I say *good dog* to you. Outside, the woman walks on, carrying the whole cold street without consenting to carry it.

The vines scratch at the window.

The chimes keep naming the wind.

The hungry customer receives a loaf warm enough to fog the bag, and for one moment everyone’s hands become visible—reaching, withholding, peeling, paying, climbing.

We yellow dogs drink the bitter coffee.

We do not bark.

Then we do.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dreamlike, erotic piece of flash fiction in which the narrator repeatedly urges a lover to come over, imagines needing extra ears, hands, and mouths, and contrasts intimate breakfast rituals with a threatening world outside.
counterfactuals.output:
Come over.

Come over before the city remembers our names. Before the sirens begin combing the streets with their blue teeth, before the headlines hatch their daily swarm of knives. Come while the moon is still caught in the telephone wires, trembling like a silver animal.

I am waiting in the kitchen, barefoot, grown, and feverishly awake. The kettle keeps whispering your secrets. The bread has browned itself into little doors.

Come over.

I need more ears for you—one at my throat, one in each palm, a small pink shell opening beneath my ribs—because your voice arrives from everywhere at once. Through the pipes. Through the radiator. Through the dark green leaves of the houseplants, which lean toward me whenever you say my name.

I need more hands. Two to hold your face, two to unbutton the long night from your body, two to keep the windows shut against the weather. Another hand to stir honey into your coffee. Another to press against the door when the world outside throws its shoulder against it.

And mouths—darling, I need mouths enough for every hunger. One to kiss you. One to tell you what I dreamed. One to taste the salt at your wrist. One to remain silent, open in wonder, when you step inside and the whole apartment shifts closer around us.

Come over.

We will make breakfast at midnight. You will crack eggs into the blue bowl, and I will stand behind you, breathing in the warm scent of your hair. Flour will settle on our skin like pale weather. Jam will shine on the spoon, red as a warning, sweet as a wound we choose.

Outside, the towers sharpen themselves. Armored clouds drag their bellies over the rooftops. Somewhere, men in clean rooms move pins across maps. Somewhere, a mouth on a screen explains why fear is necessary.

But here you will feed me a slice of pear.

Here I will lick honey from your thumb.

Here the coffee will be dark and merciful, and our knees will touch beneath the table as if by accident, then remain touching as if by law.

Come over now.

The lock is dreaming of your key. The sheets have become a warm country with no borders. I have grown all these impossible hands, these listening ears, these thirsty mouths, and every one of them is waiting.

By morning, perhaps the world will still be there, pacing and furious.

We will give it nothing.

We will close the curtains, butter the toast, and begin again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a contemporary prose poem with fragmented associations, repetition, and vivid sensory details. Include summer being “eaten” by the cold, breakfast left to burn, ambiguous kitchen noises, absurd encounters with men, and end with the command “Open your mouth.”
counterfactuals.output:
By October the cold has eaten summer down to the rind. You can see its teeth marks in the garden chairs, the blue plastic pool furred with leaves, the tomatoes split open like small red clocks.

Inside, breakfast is left to burn.

Toast blackens in the toaster. Butter loosens in its dish. The eggs tighten their yellow fists while something in the kitchen clicks, pauses, clicks again. The refrigerator, maybe. The pipes. A spoon shifting its weight in the sink.

I call your name.

The kettle answers in steam.

On the way to the store, a man in a silver tracksuit asks if I have seen his horse. He is holding a goldfish in a sandwich bag. No, I say, though behind him the traffic lifts its dark mane.

At the pharmacy, another man unfolds himself from the blood-pressure machine and offers me half a peach. It is January. The peach smells of August, of wasps drunk under picnic tables, of sunscreen and hot coins.

Summer, summer: already swallowed.

Back home, smoke has written its brief scripture across the ceiling. The alarm keeps repeating one bright syllable. The walls listen. From the kitchen comes a soft knocking, then laughter, then the unmistakable sound of a drawer being opened by no one.

I stand in the doorway with the peach in my hand.

Cold juice runs along my wrist.

Open your mouth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
